A seat is one sampling station on a river inlet. The applicant files a permit, a station id and coordinates, moors a buoy dyed with a registered pigment so a survey flight can find it, and sends four filtered water samples a year for eDNA sequencing. The node keeps every haplotype and refuses a second station at a claimed inlet, and any sequence already on file.

Gear runs 4,200 dollars and the permit 9,000, so fifty clones need fifty inlets, near 700,000 dollars before one reading holds.

Two towns see the same green water; the grit in it still names which bank it left.
